questions.q: According to the lecture, which scales are classified as numerical (scale) data?

options.e: Correct. Interval and ratio are numerical (scale) data; nominal and ordinal are categorical.
Wrong. Nominal and ordinal are categorical.
Wrong. Nominal is categorical, so this pair mixes categorical and numerical.
Wrong. Ordinal is categorical, so this pair mixes categorical and numerical.

questions.q: Which is the only mathematical procedure typically used with nominal scale data?

options.e: Wrong. Ranking needs an order, which nominal data do not have.
Wrong. Addition needs numerical values.
Correct. With nominal data you can only count how many fall in each category.
Wrong. Division needs numerical values.

questions.q: Select from the following, the variable which can be measured on a nominal scale :

options.e: Wrong. Height in cm is a ratio-scale measurement.
Correct. Ethnic group consists of unordered named categories, so it is nominal.

options.t: Age categorized as young, middle-aged or old.
options.e: Wrong. Young, middle-aged and old have an order, so this is ordinal.
Wrong. Age in years is numerical (ratio).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a nominal-scale variable?

options.e: Nominal. Blood group has no order.
Nominal. Religion has no order.
Nominal. Eye colour has no order.
Correct. Cancer stages I to IV have a meaningful order, so they are ordinal, not nominal.

questions.q: Blood group (A, B, AB, O) is best described as a:

options.e: Wrong. A dichotomous variable has only two categories.
Correct. Blood group has four unordered categories, so it is polychotomous (multinomial).
Wrong. The four groups have no order.
Wrong. Blood group has no true zero or numerical meaning.

questions.q: A categorical variable has 5 categories. How many dummy variables are needed to represent it?

options.e: Wrong. Three dummies represent only four categories.
Wrong. Using one dummy per category is redundant; one category must be the reference.
Wrong. More dummies than categories is not possible.
Correct. A variable with k categories needs k minus 1 dummy variables, so 5 categories need 4.

questions.q: Which statement about dummy variables is NOT correct?

options.t: They are dichotomous variables coded 0 and 1.
options.e: True. Dummy variables are dichotomous and coded 0 and 1.

options.t: The omitted category serves as the reference group.
options.e: True. The omitted category is the reference group.

options.t: The number 1 means "more" than the number 0.
options.e: Correct. This statement is NOT correct: 1 only means the characteristic is present, not that there is 'more' of it.

options.t: A value of 1 represents the presence of the characteristic.
options.e: True. A value of 1 represents the presence of the characteristic.

questions.q: The ordinal scale differs from the nominal scale because its categories:

options.t: Can be ranked in a meaningful order
options.e: Correct. Ordinal categories can be ranked in a meaningful order, which nominal categories cannot.
Wrong. A true zero belongs to the ratio scale.
Wrong. Equal intervals belong to interval and ratio scales.

options.t: Are expressed in units of measurement
options.e: Wrong. Units of measurement belong to numerical scales.

questions.q: Patient status classified as "unimproved, stable, improved" is measured on which scale?

options.e: Wrong. Nominal categories have no order, but these do.
Wrong. Ratio data are measured in units with a true zero.
Correct. 'Unimproved, stable, improved' are ordered categories with unequal or unknown spacing.
Wrong. Interval data have equal spacing between values.

questions.q: Why is the Glasgow Coma Scale considered an ordinal variable?

options.t: Its categories can be ordered, but the intervals between them are unequal or unknown
options.e: Correct. The categories are ordered, but the gaps between scores are unequal or unknown, which makes it ordinal.
Wrong. An absolute zero would make it a ratio scale.
Wrong. It is not measured in physical units.
Wrong. Its categories can be ordered.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT appropriate for ordinal data?

options.e: Appropriate. The median suits ordinal data.
Appropriate. The mode suits ordinal data.
Appropriate. The interquartile range suits ordinal data.
Correct. The mean needs equal intervals, so it is not appropriate for ordinal data.

questions.q: A scale with order and equal distances between points, but no true zero, is:

options.e: Wrong. Ordinal data have order but not equal distances.
Correct. An interval scale has order and equal distances but no true zero.
Wrong. Nominal data have no order.
Wrong. A ratio scale has a true zero.

questions.q: Temperature in Celsius is an interval scale because:

options.t: Zero does not represent the absence of temperature
options.e: Correct. Zero in Celsius is arbitrary and does not mean no temperature, so it is interval.
Wrong. Celsius can be ranked.
Wrong. Celsius has no absolute zero, which is why it is not ratio.

options.t: Ratios between its values are meaningful
options.e: Wrong. Ratios are not meaningful on the Celsius scale, so 20 degrees is not twice 10.

questions.q: All of the following are interval-scale variables EXCEPT:

options.e: Interval. Celsius has an arbitrary zero.
Interval. Calendar years have no true zero.
Interval. Fahrenheit has an arbitrary zero.
Correct. Weight in kilograms has a true zero, so it is a ratio-scale variable.

questions.q: Which scale has an absolute, non-arbitrary zero?

options.e: Correct. The ratio scale has an absolute, non-arbitrary zero.
Wrong. The interval scale's zero is arbitrary.
Wrong. Ordinal data have no numerical zero.
Wrong. Nominal data have no zero.

questions.q: A pulse rate of 120 is twice a pulse rate of 60. This statement is meaningful only on which scale?

options.e: Wrong. Ratios are meaningless for ordinal data.
Correct. Saying that 120 is twice 60 requires a true zero, so it is meaningful only on the ratio scale.
Wrong. Nominal data cannot be compared as ratios.
Wrong. Interval data have no true zero, so ratios are not meaningful.

questions.q: Which scale gives differences but not ratios (no natural starting point)?

options.e: Wrong. The ratio scale gives both differences and ratios.
Wrong. Nominal data give neither.
Wrong. Ordinal data give order but not meaningful differences.
Correct. The interval scale gives meaningful differences but, with no natural starting point, no ratios.

questions.q: Which operations make sense for ordinal variables?

options.e: Too limited. Counting is allowed, but ranking is also possible.
Correct. Ordinal data allow counting and ranking only.
Wrong. Addition and subtraction need equal intervals.
Wrong. All four operations need a ratio scale.

questions.q: The characteristic question "By how many units do A and B differ?" belongs to which scale?

options.e: Wrong. Nominal data cannot be subtracted to give a difference.
Wrong. Ordinal data show order only, not how far apart values are.
Correct. The question 'By how many units do A and B differ?' needs equal intervals, which is the interval scale.
Not the best fit here. Ratio data also give differences, but the characteristic question for the ratio scale is 'how many times?'

questions.q: A sample of 400 Regina households is selected and several variables are recorded. Which of the following statements is correct?

options.t: Total household income (in $) is interval level data.
options.e: Wrong. Household income in dollars is ratio-level data (true zero), not interval.

options.t: Socioeconomic status (recorded as “low income”, “middle income”, or “high income” is nominal level data.
options.e: Wrong. Low, middle and high income are ordered, so this is ordinal, not nominal.

options.t: The number of people living in a household is a discrete variable.
options.e: Correct. The number of people in a household is counted in whole numbers, so it is discrete.

options.t: The primary language spoken in the household is ordinal level data.
options.e: Wrong. Primary language has no order, so it is nominal, not ordinal.
